The objective of the mapping exercise was to develop a map of the struggles of women defending their territory in the face of extractivism in Guatemala and to identify the role and political participation of women and the impact of extractivism in their lives.Even though the mapping isn’t exhaustive, it gives us both a historical account on how extractivism developed in Guatemala, and the current situation of extractivism and how communities and women are defending their territories and mobilizing their collective power.The mapping has now been finished, and has gone through a copyediting process. We are currently working on the design for publication. The publication is titled “Women defending territory from extractivism in Guatemala"The summit was organized following previous processes in Peru and Colombia for the recognition of indigenous women as political subjects, as well as to the advancement of the collective rights in indigenous territories in Latin America. This is a safe space where indigenous women from different territories and countries could share their words, feelings, political and organizational experience, challenges and dilemmas, strengthening both the movements and their leadership, from the power between and the power for themselves, enabling alliance building among indigenous women's organizations in Guatemala and regionally.At the summit there was an important representation of alchemists and political facilitators defending land and territory who came on behalf of their organizations, presenting their analyses of power, heart, mind, body and popular feminist education. Video documents the exploitation and extractivism by foreign investors and currupt elites on the land and people of Honduras. It looks at how women bear the brunt of poverty in the country as 86% of women in the country do not even own the land they work. LinkThe video shares organizing efforts of two WHRDs against extractives and documents their journies in protecting their ancestral land and natureThe video has been viewed 283 times and has provided for the advancement of feminist demands.Video has 187 views and has provided space for the advancement of feminist demands."In partnership with another organization, JASS co-created a learning exchange with over 70 participants between land defenders and organizations in other sectors, to provide a feminist perspective to male counterparts on women leadership and make visible the crucial role that women have played in movements and in facilitating transformative change in society. As a result:-Male supporters reflected on their power and how they have structural and social disadvantages in comparison to other genders and how that puts other genders at greater risk of violence. -They also reflected on the structural violence other genders face. -Men will take more responsibility to support women's leadership in land defending.""In partnership with land defenders from Honduras, JASS curated a Public Award of the Art Contest: Art Contest titled “Creating Looks and Resistances: Women, Art and Territory” as part of creating space for feminist perspectives, and specifically to foster dialogue on current social and political affairs that impact land defenders. The event was broadcasted on Facebook Live and was attended by 136 land defenders across generations from ages 1- 56 years old representing 10 of the provinces of the country. In total, 760 attendees came to the virtual event. Because this was a public gathering, with a wide reach it played an important role in influencing public opinion on the negative impacts of extractivism and in sharing the lives realities of land defenders."JASS created space for land defenders, which include some of those who face strong criminal charges, to share their feminist perspectives on land defending. By facilitating this conversation between JASS and the partner, JASS was able to advocate for those who face criminal charges and demonstrate feminist perspectives on a pressing issue for land defenders with power holders/key officials."Women's leadership and solutions have become more visible as a result of this episode. The video showcases that women are often at the frontline as first responders during crises. . Through sharing a variety of stories of resistance like mitigating/responding to health crises and challenging the expansion mining industries that threaten their lands and livelihoods, the Mayan women were able to share how women are critical in holding and keeping societies together. As a result, the communities where Mayan women live are now aware and have narratives to share about how women in communities are critical in fighting for basic services, providing healing and wellness and are protectors of the environment.""As part of the IFIP conference in Mesoamerica, JASS hosted a session on collective protection that was was attended by 40 allies. As part of the session, JASS centred women's experiences and created a safe space. Following the creation of a safe space, JASS worked with women to understand their demands through the use of Popular Feminist Education methodologies. As a result, JASS created:1. Transnational alliances, 2. Collective protection and solidarity resources 3. Shared ideas and lessons learned around the challenges to provide resources and financing to women indigenous defenders in traditional and restrictive forms.4. Where and what opportunities are there for donors to make changes in power, decision-making and financing strategies.5. Demonstrated the links between indigenous defenders, extractive capitalism and increase precariousness due to climate change. As a result of the influence activity, donors reached out to say they would be willing to introduce JASS to additional resources for indigenous women."JASS produced a video of change which positioned women's knowledge and leadership as an integral part of movement building. As a result, movement activists have increased awareness of feminist popular education as a methodology for movement building and strengthening, knowledge of new tools and capacity to facilitate movements to be strengthened with a feminist perspective and using feminist popular education.The Summit which brought together over 300 people from different organisations and movements that surround and protect Lake Atitlan in Guatemala. Participants shared how they have challenged extractivism with power holders so far and how they have reported incidents of illegal extractivism with community authorities and with government actors, including the Ministry of Energy and Mines, the Mayor's Office of the Municipality.The result of this summit was:-A clear analysis of the impacts of extractivism of the lake on communities (including open-pit mining licenses and threats and violence of WHRDs and anyone who protects their land)-New and shared strategies for indigenous people to defend against extractivism -Strategies for self-care and collective care using rituals and art-Understanding of the power of narratives, particularly narratives of women in the communities-New organisational and training processes
